_note: Fictional composite communication-practice cases for the MS3 psychiatry clerkship. Do not include PHI. Cases marked draft require faculty review before use as graded material.

cases.title: Ask About Suicide Directly
cases.learnerGoal: Use plain, direct language without softening or avoiding the question.
cases.prompt: A patient admitted after worsening depression says, "I do not want to be a burden anymore." What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Ask directly, using the patient's words, while keeping your voice calm and matter-of-fact.
mustInclude: Reflect the burden phrase briefly
Use the words "killing yourself" or "ending your life" plainly
Pause and leave room for an answer
avoid: Euphemisms, reassurance before assessment, or arguing that life is worth living
rapidDrill.starter: Begin with "When you say..." and then ask the direct safety question.

choices.text: Are you saying you feel sad, or is this more about stress?
choices.feedback: This stays vague. It may feel gentle, but it avoids the safety question the patient just opened.

choices.text: When you say you do not want to be a burden, have you had thoughts of killing yourself?
choices.feedback: Best choice. It is direct, nonjudgmental, and connected to the patient's own words.

choices.text: You should not think that way; your family cares about you.
choices.feedback: This can shame the patient and close the conversation. Start with direct assessment and validation.

cases.title: Validate Psychosis Without Colluding
cases.learnerGoal: Acknowledge fear without agreeing with the delusional belief.
cases.prompt: A patient whispers, "The cameras in the vents are watching me." What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Validate the fear, state your own perception, and invite safety-focused exploration.
mustInclude: Name that the experience sounds frightening
Avoid agreeing that cameras are present
Offer to understand what would help the patient feel safer
avoid: Debating reality, mocking the belief, or asking questions that deepen the delusional frame
rapidDrill.starter: Try a sentence that starts with the feeling before it addresses the belief.

choices.text: There are no cameras. That is not real.
choices.feedback: This may be factually true, but it can sound dismissive and increase guardedness.

choices.text: That sounds frightening. I do not see cameras, but I want to understand what you are experiencing and help you feel safer here.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It validates emotion, avoids collusion, and invites more assessment.

choices.text: Who put the cameras there?
choices.feedback: This can deepen the delusional frame. Ask about experience, distress, safety, and meaning instead.

cases.title: Respond to Guardedness
cases.learnerGoal: Lower the threat level, name choice, and explain confidentiality limits without pressuring disclosure.
cases.prompt: A patient crosses their arms and says, "I know whatever I say will just be used against me." What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Lower pressure by naming choice, confidentiality limits, and your role in safety.
mustInclude: Say the patient can choose what to answer
Name the real limits to confidentiality (imminent risk to self/others, mandated reporting) — not routine team sharing
Invite what would make the conversation feel safer
avoid: Arguing that no one is using information against them or threatening consequences as the opener
rapidDrill.starter: Use one sentence to give the patient more control before asking for more information.

choices.text: No one is using anything against you. I just need you to answer the questions.
choices.feedback: This argues with the fear and adds pressure. Guardedness usually softens when you name choice and explain the frame.

choices.text: You get to choose what you answer. Our team shares information to care for you, so what you tell me isn't a secret I keep from them — that's not a breach of confidentiality. What I would have to share more widely is an immediate risk to your safety or someone else's, or something the law requires me to report. My goal right now is to understand what would help you feel safer here.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It respects autonomy, distinguishes routine team care-coordination from the real limits to confidentiality (imminent risk to self or others, mandated reporting, court order), and keeps the conversation oriented toward safety and care.

choices.text: If you will not talk, the team will have to make decisions without you.
choices.feedback: This may be true in some situations, but as an opening response it sounds coercive and can confirm the patient's fear.

choices.text: What are you worried might happen if you tell me more?
choices.feedback: This can be helpful after you establish choice and confidentiality limits. Alone, it may feel like another demand.

cases.title: Repair After a Limit
cases.learnerGoal: Set a clear limit while preserving dignity and alliance.
cases.prompt: After you explain that an early discharge is not planned today, the patient says, "You people never listen. I am done talking." What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Repair the rupture without walking back the clinical limit.
mustInclude: Name that the patient feels unheard
Keep the discharge limit clear
Offer one concrete way to slow down and listen
avoid: Making calmness a condition for being heard or responding with cold technical accuracy
rapidDrill.starter: Try: validate first, limit second, repair offer third.

choices.text: If you refuse to talk, that is your choice.
choices.feedback: This is technically true but relationally cold. It escalates distance after a rupture.

choices.text: I hear that this feels like we are not listening. I cannot promise discharge today, but I can slow down and make sure I understand what matters most to you.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It validates, keeps the limit, and offers repair.

choices.text: You need to calm down before we continue.
choices.feedback: This often sounds controlling. Name the emotion and the limit without making calmness a precondition for being heard.

cases.title: Repair a BPD Rupture
cases.learnerGoal: Validate the feeling, own the interactional impact, and return to a consistent plan.
cases.prompt: A patient with chronic suicidality says, "You wrote that I was manipulative. I knew you were just like everyone else." What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Address impact before accuracy, then invite collaboration on language.
mustInclude: Acknowledge that the note felt hurtful or invalidating
Avoid defending yourself as the first move
Invite a shared look at how to describe the crisis accurately
avoid: Using formulation terms like splitting or manipulation at the patient during the rupture
rapidDrill.starter: Start with the effect of the words, not your intent.

choices.text: I did not mean it that way, and that is not what the note says.
choices.feedback: This may be accurate, but it leads with self-defense. First address the rupture and the patient's experience.

choices.text: I am sorry that what you read landed that way. I can see why it felt hurtful. I want to understand what felt most invalidating, and then we can look together at how to describe the crisis accurately.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It repairs impact without abandoning accuracy, and it invites collaboration on language and meaning.

choices.text: This is exactly the kind of splitting we are trying to avoid.
choices.feedback: Using formulation language at the patient in a rupture is shaming and escalates distrust.

choices.text: Let's focus on your discharge plan instead of the note.
choices.feedback: This avoids the relational injury. Discharge planning will go better after the rupture is named and repaired.

cases.title: Medication Ambivalence
cases.learnerGoal: Use motivational interviewing instead of persuasion reflex.
cases.prompt: A patient says, "I know the antipsychotic helped, but I hate the weight gain. I am not taking it after discharge." What do you say next?

mustInclude: Validate the weight-gain concern
Ask what the medicine helped with
Ask what would need to change for treatment to feel acceptable
avoid: Threats, lectures, or closing the decision before the patient's values are clear
rapidDrill.starter: Try one reflective sentence followed by one open question.

choices.text: If you stop it, you will probably be hospitalized again.
choices.feedback: This may be intended as education, but it starts with threat. Explore values and tradeoffs first.

choices.text: It makes sense that weight gain would make you hesitant. What did you notice the medicine helped with, and what would need to be different for it to feel worth taking?
choices.feedback: Best choice. It reflects ambivalence and elicits the patient's own reasons, concerns, and conditions.

choices.text: There are no side-effect-free medications, so we have to accept some tradeoff.
choices.feedback: This is too clinician-centered. The next step is collaborative exploration, not closing the decision.

choices.text: Would it be okay if we compare a few options, including changing the dose, switching medicines, and making a monitoring plan for weight and labs?
choices.feedback: This is useful once the patient feels heard. Start with reflection and evocation, then offer options with permission.

cases.title: Offer a Sleep-Restoring Plan in Mania
cases.learnerGoal: Use calm structure, offer choices, and connect sleep to the patient's goal without debating grandiosity.
cases.prompt: A manic patient pacing the hallway says, "I do not need sleep. I need my laptop so I can finish the company launch tonight." What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Validate urgency, state the safety limit, and offer low-stimulation sleep choices.
mustInclude: Name the patient's energy or urgency without endorsing the grandiose plan
State the laptop or stimulation limit plainly
Offer two or three concrete choices that point toward sleep
avoid: Debating whether the launch is real, threatening security early, or calling the patient manic as the opener
rapidDrill.starter: Use a calm, concrete structure: urgency, limit, choices.

choices.text: That does not make sense. You are manic and need medication.
choices.feedback: This is confrontational and likely to escalate. Avoid debating insight when the immediate goal is safety, sleep, and collaboration.

choices.text: You have a lot of energy and the launch feels urgent. Tonight the safest plan is no laptop and a quieter space. We can choose together between a warm drink, a low-stimulation room, or medicine to help your body sleep.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It validates urgency without colluding, states the limit, and offers concrete choices that point toward sleep.

choices.text: If you keep pacing, security will have to get involved.
choices.feedback: Threatening consequences too early can escalate. Name the limit and offer choices before moving up the safety ladder, unless there is imminent danger.

choices.text: Tell me more about the company launch.
choices.feedback: Curiosity can build alliance, but here it risks extending activation. Pair brief listening with a sleep-focused structure.

cases.title: Open a Family Meeting
cases.learnerGoal: Create structure, consent boundaries, and a shared goal at the start.
cases.prompt: The patient has consented to a family meeting. The family arrives anxious and starts asking rapid-fire questions. What do you say first?

rapidDrill.stance: Join the anxiety, set consent boundaries, and create a shared agenda before details.
mustInclude: Acknowledge that there is a lot the family wants to understand
Name what the patient has consented to discuss
Set one shared goal for the meeting
avoid: Launching into answers before structure or shutting the room down with confidentiality alone
rapidDrill.starter: Open by orienting the room before answering the first question.

choices.text: Let me answer each question in order.
choices.feedback: This is responsive but unstructured. The meeting can become a long Q&A without goals or boundaries.

choices.text: I can see there is a lot you want to understand. Before details, let's agree on the goal, what the patient has consented for us to discuss, and what we need to decide before discharge.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It joins emotionally, names consent, and sets a structure.

choices.text: We cannot discuss much because of confidentiality.
choices.feedback: Confidentiality matters, but this response shuts down collaboration. State the consent boundary and what can be discussed.

cases.title: Ask Better Collateral Questions
cases.learnerGoal: Ask for baseline, timeline, safety, and functional change rather than global impressions.
cases.prompt: You call a patient's sister for collateral. She says, "He has just not been himself." What do you ask next?

rapidDrill.stance: Turn a vague collateral concern into baseline, timeline, function, and safety data.
mustInclude: Ask what the patient is like at baseline
Ask what changed and when it changed
Ask for specific safety or functional concerns
avoid: Asking for the family's conclusion before gathering concrete observations
rapidDrill.starter: Use one bundled question that asks for baseline, change, timing, and risk.

choices.text: Do you think he is safe to come home?
choices.feedback: This asks for a conclusion before gathering facts. First define baseline, timeline, and concrete risks.

choices.text: What is he like at baseline, what changed, when did it change, and what specific safety concerns have you noticed?
choices.feedback: Best choice. It turns a vague concern into time course, baseline, and safety data.

choices.text: Has he been taking his medication?
choices.feedback: Medication adherence is useful, but it is too narrow as the first follow-up to a broad change-from-baseline concern.

cases.title: De-escalate Family Conflict Around Discharge
cases.learnerGoal: Validate fear, protect confidentiality, and shift the room from blame to concrete safety tasks.
cases.prompt: A parent says, "If you discharge him, it will be your fault if something happens." The patient looks down and stops talking. What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Validate fear without promising zero risk, then move the room toward concrete safety planning.
mustInclude: Name the parent's fear
Avoid promising certainty or zero risk
Invite the specific safety steps that must be in place before discharge
avoid: Defensiveness, blame, or questions that shame the patient in front of family
rapidDrill.starter: Start with fear, then shift from blame to the next safety task.

choices.text: We would never discharge someone unless we were sure nothing bad could happen.
choices.feedback: This promises certainty the team cannot provide. It also sets up false reassurance instead of a realistic risk plan.

choices.text: I hear how scared you are, and I do not want to minimize that. We cannot promise zero risk, but we can slow down, hear what worries you most, and name the specific safety steps that must be in place before discharge.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It validates fear, avoids a false guarantee, and turns conflict into a concrete safety-planning task.

choices.text: The decision is ultimately up to the doctors, so let's move on.
choices.feedback: This shuts down collateral and increases adversarial tension. The family may hold key safety and feasibility information.

choices.text: Can you tell us exactly what you think he is hiding from us?
choices.feedback: Specific concerns matter, but as worded this presumes the patient is deceptive and cross-examines him through his family — in the room, right after he has gone quiet. There is no timing that rescues it. Ask the family what they are worried about instead, and keep the patient a participant rather than the subject of the inquiry.

cases.title: Respond When the Patient Questions Why You're Asking
cases.topic: Guardedness directed at the interview itself
cases.setting: First encounter, guarded or paranoid inpatient
cases.learnerGoal: Meet suspicion about the interview itself with a smaller, lower-stakes opening rather than repeating or justifying the original question.
cases.prompt: You introduce yourself and ask what brought them to the hospital. Without looking up, the patient says, "Why do you want to know that?" What do you say next?

rapidDrill.stance: Meet suspicion with validation and a smaller question, not a bigger explanation.
mustInclude: Name that the suspicion is reasonable — don't argue with it
State your role in one short sentence
Trade the original broad question for a smaller, lower-stakes one
avoid: A long justification or promise about your intentions as the opener
rapidDrill.starter: Answer their question in one sentence, then ask something smaller than your first question.

choices.text: I'm just doing my job — I ask everyone this, it's nothing personal, I promise I'm not trying to catch you out or anything.
choices.feedback: Over-explaining and promising reassurance reads as anxious, not trustworthy, and can confirm there's something to defend against. The long justification also costs you the small question that would actually move things forward.

choices.text: That's a fair question. I'm a medical student on the team here to understand how you're doing, at whatever pace works for you. We don't have to start with the whole story — is it okay if I just ask how last night went for you?
choices.feedback: Best choice. It treats the suspicion as reasonable, states your role plainly, hands back control over pace, and swaps the broad question for a small, low-stakes one a guarded patient can answer.

choices.text: What brought you to the hospital?
choices.feedback: Repeating the question ignores what the patient just told you: the question itself felt threatening. Without a smaller opening, most guarded patients stay silent or answer in one word.

choices.text: I understand you might not want to talk, but I do need to know what's going on with you so we can help.
choices.feedback: Better than arguing, but "I need to know" still centers your need over the patient's control, and the ask stays broad. Name the choice explicitly and narrow the question.

cases.title: Name Uncertainty on Rounds
cases.topic: Oral presentation — naming what is not yet known
cases.setting: Morning rounds, hospital day 1, diagnosis not yet settled
cases.learnerGoal: State a leading formulation while explicitly naming what remains unknown and what would resolve it, instead of overclaiming certainty or trailing off.
cases.prompt: You're presenting a patient on rounds. Your attending asks, "So what do you think is going on?" — but you're genuinely torn between two possibilities. What do you say?

rapidDrill.stance: Give a leading hypothesis, name the real competing one, and say what would resolve it.
mustInclude: State a specific leading formulation, not a vague impression
Name the one competing possibility that's still genuinely live
Say what finding or result would resolve it, and when
avoid: Stating either possibility as settled fact
Stopping at "I don't know" with nothing further
rapidDrill.starter: In one breath: my leading thought is X, but I haven't ruled out Y, and Z will tell us which.

choices.text: I think it's bipolar disorder — she's manic.
choices.feedback: Overclaiming certainty can send the team down the wrong path, and trust erodes when the real picture emerges. If the differential is genuinely open, say so; the team would rather know.

choices.text: My leading formulation is bipolar mania, given the decreased sleep and grandiosity — but I haven't ruled out a substance-induced picture, and the toxicology is still pending. I'm watching the trajectory over the next 24 hours and I'll flag it as soon as the tox screen is back.
choices.feedback: Best choice. It gives the team a working answer, names the real competing possibility, and says what specific information would resolve it and when. That's what naming uncertainty sounds like.

choices.text: Um, I'm not really sure yet.
choices.feedback: Honest, but it gives the team nothing to act on. Naming uncertainty well means saying what you think, what's still open, and what would settle it, not stopping at "I don't know."

choices.text: It could be bipolar mania or it could be substance-induced — I'm not sure which.
choices.feedback: Better than overclaiming or going blank, but it stops short of a working answer. Push one step further: name your leading hypothesis and what would change your mind.
